paper_title: WM^MLLM: Turning MLLMs into World Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video world models keep the world in the context of a generator, so a revisit is synthesized again and earlier edits can drift or disappear. We present WM^MLLM, the first interactive world model built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), for persistent, editable world generation from a single image. WM^MLLM keeps the world state outside every generator, as a panorama with a revision history, and lets the MLLMs write it: they turn each request into operations on this state, select where a local edit is written, and check every candidate before it becomes the next state. Image generators only propose views, and video only presents them. Users can walk to new places and return, edit objects through text or a box, place subjects, and change lighting, weather or season. By construction, a revisit at the same revision reproduces the earlier view exactly, a local edit leaves every panorama pixel outside its region unchanged, and each request starts from the result of the previous one. Against six world model baselines on MBench-A, WM^MLLM has the highest mean on all four environment-recovery metrics (Epipolar 91.5 versus 0.1 to 74.0) and completes the most camera round trips (85.3% versus at most 50.9%). It has the best value in all 15 CompBench columns against 15 baselines. On 112 local edits judged blind, selecting the region to write after generation raises completion from 34.8% to 83.0%. On 258 WBench and MBench-A items, all 46 revisits recover their earlier views, and all 97 local edits that pass the check leave panorama pixels outside their region unchanged.

sections.content: A user opens container, relights the room and turns away. Turning back should show the open container under the new light (figure 1). world model keeps persistent state of its environment that actions update [1], so an interactive world model needs three properties: revisit shows the content saved there (return), local edit changes nothing outside its region (locality), and every request builds on the result of the previous one (persistence). Where the world lives decides whether these properties hold. World models for control, such as vision-language-action models [9, 10] and joint-embedding predictive architectures [11], output actions or embeddings and no editable images. 2.1 World Representation and Memory
Video world models maintain interaction by conditioning new frames on actions and visual context. Ge-
nie 3 supports navigation and promptable events [2], and LongLive updates its context cache when the
prompt changes [5]. Camera-aware context improves spatial continuity through memory retrieval in Matrix-
Game 3.0 [3], RGB-D generation in HunyuanWorld-Voyager [17], and reframing of historical observations in
HY-WorldPlay [4]. WorldDirector adds planning of object and camera trajectories by a language model and
preserves the appearance of dynamic objects that leave and return [18]. Genie 4 uses Gemini models to plan
and verify steps on the frames it generates [19].
sections.content: Memory extends the visual context available to these generators. WorldMem retrieves frames by pose and time [20], Context-as-Memory by field-of-view overlap [21], and VMem through surfel index [22]. AlayaEVOKE maintains geometry bank indexed by camera [23], while ActWorld stores event and object tokens with visual anchors in memory of constant capacity [24]. Other approaches use spatial or planar memories or compress visual context [2528]. Persistent Computational State saves and restores the generators runtime state [29]. These memories condition new synthesis on return. Explicit 3D worlds support rendering and editing through scene representations. HunyuanWorld 1.0 reconstructs mesh from panoramic proxy [6], and WonderWorld connects scenes through Gaussian surfels [7]. Marble edits and expands persistent navigable worlds by region, including weather, time of day and season [8]. HOLODECK 2.0 and PERSIST update assets or latent 3D state [30, 31]. State updates from language also appear in WorldWeave, whose video synthesis reads an explicit 3D world [32], and StateFlow, which translates intent into transitions of persistent 3D state [33]. sections.title:
2.2 MLLM Planning and Feedback
Visual agents connect language planning, image generation and feedback. Yang et al.’s WorldGPT expands
a request, edits a target image and animates the initial and final frames [35]. GenArtist plans through
tool trees [36], and EditAgent routes steps to general and task-specific editors and then judges parallel
candidates [37]. Agent Banana retains the editing paths that pass its checks, rolls back image history and
edits layers in isolation [38].
IMAGAgent corrects multi-turn edits through feedback from several VLM
experts [39]. Ge et al.’s WorldGPT learns multimodal state transitions [40], and World Agent tests whether
language models update an explicit world state from events in an ongoing narrative [41].
sections.content: Agentic video systems connect this feedback to worlds that change over time. LingBot-World v2 uses vision-language director for semantic rules, events and environmental changes, with SAM tracking objects for interaction [42]. Regions that leave its context window tend to be regenerated on return. AgiWorld updates world state from video chunks stored with geometry in spatial memory [43]. ATAS adds clips to scene and event memories after review and state checks [44]. WMMLLM gives MLLMs control over edits and navigation in panorama state, and its transition videos read the endpoints of each turn.

sections.title:
2.3 Image Editing and Consistency
Image editors such as Nano Banana and GPT-Image follow complex instructions [12–14]. Spherical editors
extend this capability to panoramas. SE360 and World-Shaper edit spherical imagery [45, 46], FocusDiff edits
regions of indoor panoramas [47], and Mover360 moves, inserts and removes objects [48]. ZONE extracts the
region that an edit changes as a layer and blends it into the source image [49]. WMMLLM selects the support
from the source and the proposal to cover the old and new footprints of an object and their effects. It installs
this region in a world that later operations navigate, revisit and edit again.
sections.content: CompBench measures local, multi-object and implicit-reasoning edits [50]. Scene-memory benchmarks measure recovery after the camera leaves and returns [51, 52], while WRBench tests whether events evolve outside the view [53]. WorldFoundry provides infrastructure for inference and evaluation across video, 3D, 4D and interactive world systems [1]. We evaluate both image editing and scene recovery. Table 1 compares world representations, MLLM planning, object edits, exact return and edit checks.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: WMMLLM stores each scene as panorama with local patches and revision history. deterministic renderer produces its views (figure 2). GPT-6.1-sol plans operations, selects the support of local edits, checks candidates and records observations. GPT-Image proposes endpoint images, and Sol-H3 generates transition videos. The executor applies each operation through one of five routes, and each route changes fixed part of the state  (table 2)  . The state after each turn becomes the source of the next turn, and these update rules give return, locality and persistence.

Three properties follow from table 2 and equation (5). A rotation or revisit reads its endpoint from the state,

The revisit reuses the image in the state after checking that the hashes of the panorama state and arrival view agree; revisit from another scene is also compared with deterministic render of the same state, camera and profile. With B, the earlier patches, the camera and the profile fixed, it also keeps every pixel of the render whose ray has zero alpha in the new patch. Proof. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We use two public benchmarks, ablations on fixed image proposals and session studies. MBench-A measures environment memory [51]; 224 of our 227 environment items have video from all six baselines, public world models conditioned on actions. CompBench [50] measures image editing on 2,709 GPT-Image proposals across local, multi-object and implicit-reasoning edits. We score all methods with the same public MBench evaluator, which preserves the ranking of the six baselines on 30 items per baseline. The benchmark run contains 158 WBench [55] navigation items and 100 MBench-A causal items, with 817 segments. Two paired studies with sessions of eight turns examine observation memory, the planner, the source of the next state and the endpoint check. blind Claude Opus 5.5 judge assesses camera motion, edits and session outcomes from frame samples. Appendices A2 and A3.3 give the protocols.

sections.title: 5 Limitations
sections.content: The main limitation is that WMMLLM does not complete every request: 276 of the 280 failure holds of the benchmark run follow rejection of the final endpoint, and these holds raise appearance scores while the motion in the request is missing. The endpoint verifier also passes some partial changes and rejects some complete ones: blind judge labels as complete 190 of the 309 endpoints that pass the verifier and 83 of the 276 that it rejects (appendix A4). Because each request starts from the endpoint of the preceding one, an error carries forward: the next segment completes in 100 of 153 cases after correct endpoint commits and in 25 of 95 after an incorrect one. Weak camera motion and incorrect placement relations also cause failures. Figure 9 shows motorcycle that stays beside the slide and coastal view that shifts in the wrong direction. The panorama represents world around one camera center (appendix A4). Translation and unseen regions require generation, and the generation log flags seam in 208 of the 227 environment items. Video presentation also takes median of about ten minutes from request to first playback (section 4.6). The endpoint verifier and the blind judge lack human calibration, and frame samples do not establish the motion between two samples. The session studies have wide intervals and use new scripts on worlds from earlier studies.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: WMMLLM turns MLLMs into persistent, editable world model by keeping the world state outside every generator: the MLLMs write it under update rules that give return, locality and persistence, and generators only propose. Its panorama state carries object edits, environmental changes and navigation across turns, and over 21 sequential requests in one world it keeps every earlier change. Selecting the support after generation raises the completion of local edits from 34.8% to 83.0%. WMMLLM achieves the best mean on all four MBench-A recovery metrics against six baselines, completes the most camera round trips and has the best value in all 15 CompBench columns.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: In our system, GPT-6.1-sol [15] plans operations, selects the support of local edits, checks endpoint candidates and records observations. GPT-Image 2 [13] supplies the CompBench proposals, GPT-Image 2.5 [14] generates the endpoints in the other experiments, and GPT-Image also generates the initial panoramas. Sol-H3 [16] generates the transition videos, and SoL-Refiner [54] optionally super-resolves them. Diagnostic images from earlier development also used Qwen-Image-Edit-2511. In the evaluation, Claude Opus 5.5 supplies all blind judgments and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct supplies the WBench [55] judge fields described in appendix A2.2; no human raters take part. Claude Code and OpenAI Codex serve as coding and writing assistants: they help to implement the system and the evaluation scripts, run the experiments, analyze the results, prepare the figures and tables, and draft and edit the text of this report. A5 Capability Comparison Sources The capability comparison in table 1 follows the versions that we cite and the interfaces that they document. An empty circle means that the source does not describe the capability. LingBot-World v2 describes object control with VLM and SAM and recall within its context window, without an interface for appearance editing. WorldDirector describes planning of object and camera trajectories by language model and identity memory for dynamic objects; object editing and exact scene return lie outside the interface it describes. Alaya-EVOKE describes explorer and chunk prompts, coverage of its geometry bank and revision branches, without instance editing. ActWorld describes object actions driven by text and memory of events and objects with constant capacity, without appearance editing inside mask. LongLive describes prompt recaching, frame sink and short window; its evaluations measure temporal consistency and prompt transitions. Yang et al.s WorldGPT describes text targeting and masks in workflow from endpoint images to video, without recurrent scene retrieval; it uses ChatGPT for prompt enhancement, and the source does not describe visual input to its planner. Marble describes regional, object and global style editing over persistent 3D assets and revisits of persistent 3D state through camera keyframes or an origin, without exact RGB recovery; controller and agent memory are unspecified. WorldWeave describes multimodal scene planning, geometric additions that pass checks and persistent structure, without user edits to objects already in the scene or exact RGB return. StateFlow describes persistent 3D state that it renders again and object edits that VLM plans on this state; its update procedure does not describe checking generator edits before installation or exact RGB replay. WorldAgents describes view expansion that VLM directs, checks in two stages before it adds view and renderable Gaussian scene, without object editing that user targets; its return entry applies to reconstruction that has not changed, rendered with the same camera and rendering profile. The WMMLLM entry follows the selection and scene storage code of the application and its interfaces for endpoint planning and checking.
